metadata.title: Role of secondary school students’ AI acceptance in mathematics learning in shaping academic achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a cross-sectional survey of Kathmandu district secondary students (grades 8 and 10) with stratified sampling by sex, school type (community vs institutional), and academic levels, and then selected 13 schools by random number table. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not describe weight application in the ML or SEM analyses. Because the outcomes are based on a self-developed AI acceptance scale and school-record mathematics achievement, analysts should treat the results as descriptive/predictive for the sampled schools rather than population-representative estimates unless weights are later provided. For replication, researchers should check whether the original dataset includes sampling/design weights and, if so, whether the ML models were trained with or without weight-aware estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is mathematics achievement taken from schools’ official first terminal examination records (a direct score/percentage), not an ILSA/PV-based cognitive achievement scale. Missing data handling is reported as exclusion of 32 cases with missing values and outliers, so no PV-combining strategy is required.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Cross-sectional survey in Kathmandu district, Nepal. Target population comprised students enrolled in classes 8 and 10. Sample size was 404 per category (after non-response adjustment) with stratification by sex, school type (community vs institutional), and academic levels (basic grades 1–8 vs secondary grades 9–12), and 13 schools were selected by random number table method. Data collection occurred Oct 2024–Jan 2025; mathematics achievement was taken from official school records (first terminal examination, academic year 2080/81). Missing values and outliers were excluded, removing 32 cases, leaving 804 for analysis.

main_findings.dataset_used: Nepal Kathmandu district survey (Grades 8 & 10) — AI acceptance scale + school-record mathematics achievement (first terminal exam, 2080/81)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest regression — Train/Validation/Test split: n(Train)=515, n(Validation)=119, n(Test)=160; Validation MSE=418.99, Test MSE=397.15, OOB error=485.61; RMSE=19.93; MAPE=49.63%; R²=0.07. Feature importance (mean decrease in accuracy): PEUA3=14.36, ATUA4=11.23, PEUA5=10.86, PUA01=10.25.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Nepal Kathmandu district survey data (Grades 8 & 10) with AI acceptance scale measures and school-record mathematics achievement, the study leveraged time using digital resources and AI acceptance constructs (perceived enjoyment, perceived usefulness, and attitude) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that the Random Forest model had low explanatory power (R²=0.07) and high prediction error (Test MSE=397.15; RMSE=19.93; MAPE=49.63%), with perceived enjoyment and attitude items contributing most to predictive accuracy. This indicates that improving students’ AI-related perceptions alone may not substantially raise mathematics scores without additional instructional and contextual supports, and that AI integration should be accompanied by pedagogy and guidance rather than treated as a direct achievement lever.

main_findings.dataset_used: Nepal Kathmandu district survey (Grades 8 & 10) — AI acceptance clusters + school-record mathematics achievement categories (Nepal grading system)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement category (multi-class; e.g., Not graded to Outstanding)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Linear discriminant classification (Moment method) — Test accuracy: 0.21 (high acceptance), 0.15 (moderate), 0.13 (low), 0.21 (total sample). AUC: 0.53 (high), 0.51 (moderate), 0.47 (low), 0.49 (total). Precision (PPV): 0.18 (high), 0.11 (moderate), 0.19 (low), 0.15 (total). Recall (TPR): 0.21 (high), 0.15 (moderate), 0.13 (low), 0.21 (total).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Nepal Kathmandu district survey data with AI acceptance cluster levels to classify students into mathematics achievement categories, the study leveraged AI acceptance level (and related acceptance constructs) to predict achievement category membership, finding that discrimination was weak (AUC < 0.6; total-sample accuracy=0.80 reported for the ROC-based evaluation but with low PPV=0.15 and high false discovery rate=0.86, indicating many false positives for predicted positives). This indicates that AI acceptance levels have limited practical value for reliably identifying which students will achieve higher mathematics categories, so policy should focus on improving learning conditions and instructional alignment rather than using acceptance as a standalone screening tool.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-sectional study in Kathmandu district, Nepal (grades 8 and 10; analytic sample N=804 after excluding 32 cases with missing values/outliers) examined how AI acceptance (TAM-based constructs: perceived enjoyment, perceived usefulness, and attitude) and time spent using digital resources relate to mathematics achievement from schools’ first terminal examination records (2080/81). The best-performing ML approach reported was Random Forest regression, but performance was modest: Test MSE=397.15, RMSE=19.93, MAPE=49.63%, and R²=0.07, with key feature importance concentrated in perceived enjoyment and attitude items. For categorical achievement, linear discriminant classification showed weak discrimination (AUC around 0.47–0.53; total-sample PPV=0.15; recall 0.21). The study does not report survey-weight use, and the ML models appear trained on a clustered school sample without explicit multilevel/survey-weight correction, limiting generalizability and interpretability. Additionally, the paper’s predictive focus does not establish causal effects of AI acceptance on achievement.
